title: How to Choose the Right Gym Equipment for a Commercial Gym
excerpt: Duty cycle, floor area and member mix decide your equipment list — not the brochure. A practical framework for specifying a commercial floor.
keywords: commercial gym equipment, how to choose gym equipment, gym equipment buying guide

body.v: Most first-time gym owners start from a wish list of machines. That is the wrong end of the problem. What decides whether your floor works two years in is the duty cycle — how many hours a day each machine actually runs, and how heavy the people using it are.
Start with duty cycle, not the machine list

A treadmill in a home is used perhaps forty minutes a day by one or two people. The same machine on a paying gym floor might run ten hours a day under a dozen different users. That difference is why commercial equipment carries heavier frames, higher continuous motor ratings, larger running surfaces and higher rated user weights.

Before you look at a single product page, write down three numbers: your expected peak concurrent users, your opening hours, and the heaviest user weight you want to design for. Everything else follows.
Split the floor into three blocks

v: Cardio. Treadmills, cross trainers, spin bikes, upright and recumbent bikes. This is where new members start and where the machines take the most punishment.

Selectorised strength. Pin-loaded stations covering the main movement patterns — chest press, shoulder press, lat pull down, seated row, leg press, leg curl and extension. Fast to use, safe for beginners, no plate handling.
Free weights and plate-loaded. Benches, racks, dumbbells, plates and plate-loaded stations. Lower cost per station, heavier top-end loading, and what your experienced members will actually queue for.

body.v: A common mistake is over-buying cardio because it fills space cheaply. Cardio has the highest failure rate and the highest service cost per unit. Budget accordingly.
Read the specification, not the adjective
Four numbers tell you most of what you need to know about a cardio machine:

v: Motor rating. Look for the continuous rating, not the peak. Avon commercial treadmills run from around 4 HP to 5.5 HP continuous.
Running area. Anything under roughly 1500 x 550 mm gets uncomfortable for taller runners. Commercial models start around 1540 x 600 mm.
Maximum user weight. This is the honest measure of frame strength. Commercial models are typically rated 180–240 kg.
Net weight. Heavier usually means more steel, and more steel usually means less flex under load.

body.v: For strength stations, the equivalents are frame tube specification, weight stack rating, cable thickness and the finish. A high-tensile steel frame with a two-round powder coating and a 6 mm cable is a very different machine from something lighter, even if the photographs look similar.
Plan the layout before you plan the purchase

Machines need clearance, not just footprint. A station with a 1850 x 1350 mm footprint needs walking space around it, room to load and unload, and enough gap that two members are not knocking elbows. As a rough planning figure, allow around 40–50% more floor area than the sum of your equipment footprints.
This is why we ask for a floor plan before quoting. It is much cheaper to move a rectangle on a drawing than to discover on installation day that the leg press blocks a fire exit.
Think about service before you think about price

Equipment downtime costs memberships. Ask three questions of any supplier: where do spares come from, how long does a typical part take to arrive, and who physically comes to site. Locally manufactured equipment generally wins on all three, because the spares chain is short.
Quantities: how many of each?

There is no universal ratio, but there is a useful method. Count your busiest hour, not your membership. If forty people are on the floor at 7 pm and a typical session is a third cardio and two thirds strength, you need roughly thirteen cardio positions and enough strength stations that nobody waits more than a set.

Then apply two corrections. First, duplicate the stations that always queue — chest press, lat pull down and leg press are the usual three. Second, resist duplicating anything exotic; a second hip abductor will sit idle while people wait for the bench.
Where new operators overspend

v: Too much cardio. It fills space cheaply and looks impressive, but it has the highest failure rate and the highest service cost per unit on the floor.
Too many single-function stations. Each one is a footprint. Dual-function and multi stations cover more patterns per square metre.
Console features. Bluetooth, app sync and large screens are pleasant and are not what fails in year three. Spend the difference on frame and motor rating.
Under-buying storage. Racks and plate trees cost little and recover real floor area. Loose weights are a hazard and a space cost.

body.v: Commissioning: what to check on handover day

Do not sign off a floor until you have physically checked each machine. Every treadmill should be levelled on the actual floor and its emergency stop key tested. Every selectorised station should run through its full range under load with the guards fitted. Every cable should be inspected at the pulleys, and every weight-stack pin should be present.

Ask the installing team to walk your staff through the maintenance routine for each machine type and leave you the model and serial numbers in writing. That list becomes your maintenance log, and it is what turns a future warranty claim into a parts order rather than an argument.
Plan for year three, not opening day

The equipment that wins is the equipment still working when the novelty has gone. Ask any supplier three questions before you commit: where do spares come from, what is a realistic wait for a common part, and who physically attends site. Equipment manufactured in India generally answers all three better than imported equipment, because the spares chain is short.

Budget an annual maintenance figure from day one. Operators who discover that cost in year two are the ones running machines with out-of-order signs on them, and an out-of-order sign in a commercial gym is seen by every member who walks past it.

faqs.q: How many treadmills do I need for a commercial gym?
faqs.a: As a planning rule, cardio typically accounts for 30–40% of equipment on a general fitness floor, with treadmills the largest share of that. The honest answer depends on peak concurrent users — count your busiest hour, not your membership list.

faqs.q: Is plate-loaded or selectorised better for a commercial gym?
faqs.a: Most floors need both. Selectorised stations are faster and safer for beginners and keep a floor moving at peak times; plate-loaded gives heavier top-end loading at a lower cost per station for experienced lifters.

title: Complete Guide to Setting Up a Gym in Maharashtra
excerpt: Site, power, access, layout and equipment — the sequence that keeps a Maharashtra gym project on schedule.
keywords: gym setup Maharashtra, open a gym in Mumbai, gym equipment Pune, commercial gym setup

body.v: Setting up a gym in Maharashtra has a few specifics that catch first-time owners out — lift access in Mumbai buildings, power provisioning for a bank of treadmills, and the gap between a landlord's floor plan and the floor you actually get.
1. Choose the site with equipment in mind
Before signing a lease, check three things that are expensive to fix later:

v: Floor loading. A selectorised station with a 100 kg stack plus frame can exceed 250 kg gross in a single footprint. Upper-floor units in older buildings need this checked.

Access. Measure the lift, the staircase turn and the main door. Commercial treadmills can exceed 2200 mm in length and 250 kg gross weight. Some equipment simply will not go up a narrow stairwell assembled.
Ceiling height. Functional trainers, smith machines and lat towers need genuine headroom. Anything under about 3 m starts to limit your options.

body.v: 2. Sort power early

Cardio is the electrical load. A row of AC treadmills each rated 4–5.5 HP continuous adds up quickly, and inverter-backed models carry their own requirements. Get your electrical contractor to size the supply against the actual machine list rather than a guess, and plan socket positions into the layout drawing — not after the machines land.
3. Draw the floor before you buy

Work in zones: cardio near ventilation and windows, selectorised strength in the middle where circulation is easiest, free weights and racks against a structural wall, and stretching or functional space where it will not be walked through. Keep a clear route from the entrance to the changing rooms that does not cross a lifting area.
We build this layout from your drawings as part of a commercial quotation, so the equipment list and the floor plan are agreed at the same time.
4. Specify for your actual member mix

A society gym in Thane, a 24-hour club in Pune and a hotel fitness room in Nagpur are three different specifications. A hotel needs compact footprint, quiet operation and finish quality. A club needs duty cycle and throughput. A society gym needs low maintenance and simple controls, because there is usually nobody supervising.
5. Plan the installation window

Equipment delivery, assembly, positioning and commissioning is a scheduled job, not a drop-off. Co-ordinate it after flooring is laid and cured but before final finishing, and make sure someone with authority is on site to sign off positions. Moving a fixed station after commissioning is avoidable work.
6. Budget for the things that are not machines

v: Gym flooring and rubber matting under free-weight areas
Mirrors, storage racks and dumbbell stands
Accessories — bars, collars, battle ropes, mats, belts
Annual maintenance and a small spares float

body.v: Accessories in particular are what a new floor runs short of in the first month. Put them in the same order as the machines.
7. Get the layout signed off before anything ships

The cheapest moment to move a machine is while it is still a rectangle on a drawing. Once a selectorised station weighing 250 kg is bolted into position on a rubber floor, moving it is a job, not an adjustment.

Agree the layout in writing, marked with clearances, circulation routes and socket positions. Everyone who will work on the site — your electrician, your flooring contractor and the installation team — should be working from the same drawing.
8. Sequence the trades correctly

v: Structural and civil work first, including any floor strengthening
Electrical first fix, with sockets positioned from the equipment layout
Ventilation and air conditioning
Flooring laid and fully cured — this is the one people rush
Mirrors and wall fixings
Equipment delivery, installation and commissioning
Signage, storage and accessories

body.v: Equipment arriving before the flooring has cured is the single most common scheduling mistake. It either delays the install or damages the floor, and both cost more than waiting.
9. Understand the Maharashtra-specific practicalities

Lift access is the recurring constraint in Mumbai, Thane and older parts of Pune. Measure the service lift internally — depth, width and height — and check its rated capacity against the gross weight of your heaviest machine, not its net weight.

Humidity along the coast and through the monsoon accelerates corrosion on anything with an inadequate finish. Powder-coated frames handle it well; unprotected fixings do not. Build a check on fixings and paintwork into your post-monsoon routine.
Power reliability varies by area. If your location sees frequent cuts, discuss it before specifying — it affects which cardio is sensible and whether backup is worth provisioning.
10. Budget the whole project, not the equipment

A realistic gym budget has five lines, and equipment is only the largest one: civil and interior work, flooring, electrical and HVAC, equipment, and the operational items (signage, storage, accessories, first aid, cleaning supplies). New operators routinely budget the fourth line and are surprised by the other four.

If the total and the brief do not meet, phase it. Equip the core floor properly and add stations as membership grows — but plan the layout for the final state, so phase two drops into space you already allowed for rather than forcing a rearrangement.
We supply, install and service across Mumbai, Thane, Navi Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and the rest of Maharashtra. See how our gym projects work.

faqs.q: How long does a commercial gym installation take?
faqs.a: For a typical floor, delivery and installation is scheduled over a few working days once the site is ready. The bigger variable is site readiness — flooring, power and access all need to be complete before equipment arrives.

faqs.q: Do you supply gym equipment outside Maharashtra?
faqs.a: Yes. Maharashtra is our primary service area, and we handle pan-India supply on project and bulk orders.

title: Commercial vs Home Gym Equipment: What Actually Differs
excerpt: The honest engineering differences between domestic and commercial machines — and when paying for commercial duty is wasted money.
keywords: commercial vs home gym equipment, domestic gym equipment, difference commercial home gym

body.v: The words "commercial" and "domestic" get used loosely. In equipment terms they describe a design target: how many hours per day the machine is expected to run, and under what load.
Frame and materials

Commercial strength stations are typically built from high-tensile steel tube with a two-round powder-coated finish and heavier-gauge sections throughout. The visible difference is small; the difference under ten years of daily loading is not. Domestic stations use lighter sections because the fatigue loading is an order of magnitude lower.
Motor and drive

In the Avon range, domestic treadmills commonly use DC or BLDC drives rated around 2–3 HP continuous, while commercial models use AC drives from roughly 4 HP up to 5.5 HP continuous. AC motors handle sustained running better and tolerate the heat of continuous operation; DC and BLDC drives are quieter and cheaper, which suits a home.
Running surface and user rating

Domestic treadmills typically offer running areas around 1200–1300 x 400–480 mm with user ratings near 110–130 kg. Commercial models step up to roughly 1540–1750 x 560–600 mm with ratings from 180 kg to 240 kg on larger units. If your users include tall runners or heavier lifters, this is the specification that matters most.
Footprint and folding

Domestic machines are designed to disappear: many fold by cylinder for storage. Commercial machines are designed to stay put and be serviced in place. A folding mechanism is a hinge, and a hinge is a wear point — which is why you rarely see one on a commercial floor.
When commercial duty is wasted money

If a machine will be used by one household for under an hour a day, commercial specification buys you durability you will never consume, at a footprint and price you will feel every day. The domestic range exists for a reason.

Conversely, "semi-commercial" equipment in a genuinely commercial setting is a false economy. Society gyms are where this goes wrong most often: unsupervised, heavily used, and equipped as though it were someone's spare room.
A simple decision rule

v: Under 1 hour/day, one or two users → domestic range
1–4 hours/day, family or small studio → heavier domestic or entry commercial
Over 4 hours/day, or unsupervised public access → commercial range, no exceptions

body.v: Console and electronics

Commercial consoles are built to be used by strangers: simple controls, clear metrics, and a layout someone can understand without instruction. Domestic consoles can afford more features — app connectivity, preset programme libraries, media playback — because one household learns them once.

Programme count is the most oversold number in the category. A machine with 64 preset programmes is not better than one with 8; most users select manual and one or two presets, then never change again. Read the motor and frame figures instead.
Serviceability

This is the difference nobody mentions in a showroom. Commercial equipment is designed to be maintained in place: guards come off, cables are replaceable, upholstery is a replaceable panel rather than a bonded assembly. Domestic equipment is designed to be affordable, which usually means fewer serviceable parts.
On a commercial floor, that matters enormously — a machine you can fix in an hour costs nothing, and a machine you have to replace costs a fortnight of member goodwill.
Noise

Domestic machines are generally quieter, which is a genuine feature when you are training at 6 am above a sleeping household or below a neighbour. AC motors, heavier frames and larger flywheels all make more noise than their domestic equivalents. If you are equipping an apartment or a hotel room adjacent to guest rooms, this belongs in the specification.
The cost comparison people get wrong

Commercial equipment costs more per unit. Over a working life on a busy floor, it is usually cheaper — because the alternative is replacing domestic equipment repeatedly, plus the downtime while you do.

The reverse is equally true. Commercial specification in a household buys durability you will never consume, in a footprint you will notice every single day, at a price you paid once. Neither is "better"; they answer different questions.
The grey area: society and studio gyms

Housing society gyms, small personal-training studios and hotel fitness rooms sit between the two definitions, and they are where specification goes wrong most often. They look like light use on paper — a few hours a day, modest user numbers — but they are unsupervised and used by many different people, which is a commercial pattern regardless of the hours.

Our recommendation for these spaces is consistent: commercial or heavy semi-commercial equipment, guided rather than free-weight where possible, and as few loose components as you can manage, because in an unsupervised room loose components disappear.
Compare the two ranges directly: commercial equipment and home gym equipment. Tick "Compare" on any product to line specifications up side by side.

faqs.q: Can I use home gym equipment in a society gym?
faqs.a: We would not recommend it. Society gyms are unsupervised and used by many households, which puts them closer to a commercial duty cycle than a domestic one, even though the hours look modest on paper.

title: What Drives the Cost of Setting Up a Gym in India
excerpt: Why a credible gym quotation is built from floor area, duty cycle and equipment mix — and what moves the number most.
keywords: gym setup cost India, cost of gym equipment, commercial gym budget

body.v: We are asked for a per-square-foot number constantly, and we do not publish one, because it is the least useful figure in the conversation. Two 2,000 sq ft gyms can differ by a multiple depending on three decisions. Here is what actually moves the cost.
1. The selectorised-to-plate-loaded ratio

This is the single biggest lever. Selectorised stations carry a weight stack, guards, cables and pulleys. Plate-loaded stations do not — you add resistance with Olympic plates you buy separately and share across the floor. A floor built heavily around plate-loaded stations costs considerably less per station, at the price of slower throughput at peak times.
2. Cardio count and specification

Cardio is usually the most expensive category per unit and the most tempting to over-buy. A treadmill with a 5.5 HP AC motor, a 1750 x 600 mm deck and a 240 kg user rating is a substantially different machine from a 4 HP unit on a smaller deck. Both are commercial; only one is necessary for most floors.
3. Duty cycle
Specifying commercial where domestic would do — or the reverse — changes the number in both directions. Getting this right is worth more than negotiating on price.
What people forget to budget

v: Flooring. Rubber matting under free weights is not optional if you want the slab and the equipment to survive.
Accessories. Bars, collars, mats, belts, ropes, storage. Individually small, collectively significant.
Plates and dumbbells. If you go plate-loaded, the plate budget is part of the equipment budget.
Electrical work. Sizing supply for a cardio bank, plus socket positions.
Maintenance. Plan an annual figure from day one rather than discovering it in year two.

body.v: How we quote

We work from your floor plan, your expected peak concurrent users and your budget range, then propose an equipment mix that fits all three. You get one quotation covering supply, delivery, installation and commissioning — not a price list you have to assemble yourself.
If your budget and your brief do not meet, we would rather tell you at drawing stage and propose a phased build than deliver a floor that is thin in every category.
4. Floor area, and what it does to the number

Area drives cost less directly than people expect. A larger floor needs more equipment, but it also needs proportionally less cramming — and cramming is expensive, because it pushes you towards compact multi stations instead of cheaper single-function equipment.

As a planning figure, allow total floor area of roughly 40–50% above the sum of your equipment footprints once circulation and clearances are included. If your area cannot absorb that, the honest answer is fewer machines, not tighter gaps.
5. New versus phased

For a first commercial floor, phasing is often the better financial decision. Equip the core properly — cardio, the main selectorised patterns, a basic free-weight area — and add stations as membership grows.

The condition is that you plan the layout for the final state from day one. Phase two should drop into space already allowed for, with power already run. A phased build planned as you go costs more than doing it once.
What a quotation should actually contain

v: An equipment schedule with model numbers, not category names
Published specifications for each model, so you can verify the duty cycle
Footprints and gross weights, so access and floor loading can be checked
A marked-up layout drawing
Delivery, installation and commissioning stated explicitly as included or not
Electrical requirements for the cardio bank
Warranty terms in writing
Lead time

body.v: A quotation that is a list of machine names and one total is not a quotation you can evaluate. You cannot tell whether you are being offered domestic equipment for a commercial floor, and that is exactly the substitution that costs money later.
Ongoing costs to model from day one

Annual maintenance, consumables (belts, cables, upholstery panels), a small spares float, and electricity for the cardio bank. None is large individually; together they are a line item, and operators who model them from the start are the ones whose equipment is still working in year four.
Where cutting costs is safe — and where it is not

Reasonable places to economise: plate-loaded instead of selectorised for part of the strength provision, fewer cardio units of better specification, phasing the functional area, buying accessories in bulk later.

Places not to: rubber flooring under free weights, electrical provisioning, the rated duty cycle of anything that runs all day, and installation. Every one of those is more expensive to fix afterwards than to do properly first.

faqs.a: Because pricing depends on configuration, quantity, site and installation scope. A published list price would be wrong for almost every project, in both directions. We quote per project instead.

title: Choosing Cardio Equipment for a Commercial Gym
excerpt: Treadmills, cross trainers, spin, upright and recumbent bikes — what each one is genuinely for, and how to balance the mix.
keywords: commercial cardio equipment, gym treadmill, commercial spin bike, cross trainer gym

body.v: Cardio sells memberships and cardio breaks first. A balanced mix matters more than buying more of whatever is cheapest.
Treadmills

The default machine, and the one members judge a gym by. Prioritise continuous motor rating, running area and user weight rating. Automatic incline widens the training range considerably; some commercial models offer a negative incline range for downhill work.
Cross trainers and ellipticals

Low-impact, full-body, and the machine you point deconditioned or returning-from-injury members towards. Stride length and flywheel behaviour determine whether the motion feels natural. They take less mechanical punishment than treadmills and generally cost less to keep running.
Spin bikes

If you run classes, spin is a business decision as much as an equipment one — a studio of bikes supports a timetable, a revenue line and a community. Look at flywheel mass, the brake system and the adjustability of saddle and handlebar, because one bike has to fit many riders.
Upright and recumbent bikes

Upright bikes are compact and familiar. Recumbent bikes, with back support and a step-through frame, are what make your floor usable for older members and rehabilitation clients — a genuinely underrated category for a general fitness gym.
Air bikes
Fan-resistance bikes scale with effort, which makes them ideal for interval and conditioning work. They are loud, so place them with that in mind.
Balancing the mix

A common general-fitness split is roughly half treadmills, a quarter cross trainers and the remainder split across bikes and conditioning pieces. Adjust for your members: a hotel needs fewer treadmills and more compact bikes; a strength-led gym needs less cardio overall but should not skip it.
Placement

Put cardio near ventilation. Leave service access behind treadmills. Keep at least one machine of each type reachable without walking through a lifting area, so members with mobility limits are not designed out of your floor.
Reading the specification sheet
Four figures tell you most of what matters, and they must be read together rather than individually:

v: Continuous motor rating. Specifications often quote two numbers, such as "5 HP / 10 HP". The first is continuous, the second is peak. Only the first describes what the machine sustains. Commercial floors start around 4 HP continuous.
Running area. Belt length governs stride comfort, belt width governs confidence at speed. Commercial models run from about 1540 mm long and 580–600 mm wide.
Maximum rated user weight. The most honest single indicator of frame and deck quality. Commercial ratings run from 180 kg to 240 kg depending on model.
Net weight. A proxy for how much steel is in the frame — and the number that decides whether the machine fits in your lift.

body.v: Resistance systems on bikes and cross trainers

Magnetic resistance is quiet, needs almost no maintenance and adjusts in steps or steplessly from the console. Fan (air) resistance scales with the rider's own effort, which makes it excellent for interval work and useless for steady-state training at a set load. Friction systems are simple and cheap but wear.
For a general fitness floor, magnetic resistance across the bike range plus one or two air bikes for conditioning covers almost every use case.
Maintenance load by category

Treadmills account for the majority of cardio service calls in almost every gym, because they have a motor, a moving deck and a belt under constant load. Cross trainers and bikes are mechanically simpler and cost noticeably less to keep running.

That should influence your mix. If your service budget is tight, a floor weighted slightly away from treadmills and towards cross trainers and bikes will cost less to operate without reducing what members can actually do.
Placement, power and ventilation

Cardio belongs near ventilation and, where possible, near windows — it is the most visible zone from the entrance and the one members spend longest in. Leave run-off space behind every treadmill for safety and for service access.

Size the electrical supply against the actual machine list rather than a rule of thumb, and mark socket positions on the layout drawing. Retro-fitting power to a cardio bank after the flooring is laid is avoidable and expensive.
Do not design out your least confident members

Keep at least one machine of each type reachable without walking through a lifting area or past a wall of mirrors. Recumbent bikes in particular should be somewhere a self-conscious beginner can use them. A floor that only works for confident members is a floor with a retention problem.

title: Treadmill Buying Guide for Gyms
excerpt: The five specifications that decide whether a gym treadmill lasts, and the marketing numbers you can safely ignore.
keywords: gym treadmill buying guide, commercial treadmill specifications, treadmill motor HP

body.v: Treadmills are the most bought and most misunderstood machine in any gym. Here is what to read on a specification sheet, in order of importance.
1. Continuous motor rating

Specifications often quote two figures, such as "5 HP / 10 HP". The first is the continuous rating and the second is peak. Only the continuous figure describes what the machine can sustain. For commercial use, look at roughly 4 HP and above continuous.
2. Running area

Belt length governs stride comfort; belt width governs confidence at speed. Domestic machines commonly sit around 1200–1300 mm long; commercial models run from about 1540 mm to 1750 mm. If you have tall runners, longer is not a luxury.
3. Maximum user weight
The most honest single indicator of build quality, because it reflects frame, deck and motor together. Commercial ratings in the Avon range run from 180 kg to 240 kg depending on model.
4. Incline range
Automatic incline turns one machine into several workouts. Commercial models typically offer 0–20% or 0–22%; some offer a negative range such as -3% to 15% for downhill training.
5. Machine weight and footprint

Net weight is a proxy for how much steel is in the frame. It also determines whether the machine can be got into your building — check net and gross weight against your lift capacity before ordering, not after.
What matters less than you think

v: Programme count. A machine with 64 preset programmes is not better than one with 8; most members use manual and one or two presets.
Console features. Bluetooth, speakers and app connectivity are pleasant. They are not what fails after three years.
Peak horsepower. Marketing. Read the continuous figure.

body.v: Maintenance planning

Belt tension, deck lubrication and motor-compartment cleanliness account for most preventable treadmill faults. Some models include a self-lubrication function on the control board; otherwise build lubrication into a scheduled routine.
Deck and cushioning

The deck is the board beneath the belt, and it is doing more work than anything except the motor. Thicker decks flex less and last longer; some are reversible, which effectively doubles their life. Cushioning systems sit between deck and frame to reduce joint loading.

You cannot usually read deck thickness from a specification sheet, but you can feel it. Stand on the belt at the centre and at the rear quarter. Meaningful flex at either point on a display unit will be worse after a year of use.
Belt quality and tracking

Commercial belts are textured for grip and built in multiple plies. A belt that drifts toward one side ("tracking") is normally an adjustment rather than a fault, but persistent drift under load points to a frame or roller problem — worth checking on any machine you are shown.
Frame, footprint and access

Check three numbers before you commit: assembled length, assembled width, and gross weight. Commercial treadmills can exceed 2200 mm long and 250 kg gross. Gross weight includes packing, and it is the figure your lift capacity has to satisfy.
This is the single most common cause of a rescheduled delivery. Measure the lift internally, measure the narrowest point of the staircase including the turn, and measure the doorway.
Inverter and power

Larger commercial treadmills use an inverter drive to manage the motor, and the inverter rating appears on some specification sheets. Practically, what you need to know is the total electrical load of your cardio bank so your contractor can size the supply. Get that number from the machine list, not from an estimate.
Safety features to insist on

v: A working magnetic safety key that cuts power when the user steps off
Adequate run-off space behind the machine, designed into the layout
Side rails that are genuinely usable at speed
A clear, immediate stop control the user can reach without looking

body.v: On an unsupervised floor — a hotel, a society gym, a 24-hour club — test every safety key on handover and then on a schedule. It is the cheapest safety check in the building.
A shortlist method that works

Write down your three constraints first: maximum assembled length that fits your space, maximum gross weight your access can take, and the minimum user weight rating you want to design for. Filter the range by those three before you look at anything else. What remains is usually a handful of models, and choosing between them on motor rating and running area is straightforward.
Every treadmill on this site lists motor rating, speed, incline, running area and user weight where the manufacturer publishes them. Compare treadmills.

faqs.q: What HP treadmill is best for a commercial gym?
faqs.a: Look at the continuous rating rather than peak. Commercial floors generally start around 4 HP continuous, with larger models up to 5.5 HP. Match it to expected running hours and user weights rather than buying the largest number available.

title: How to Plan a Small Gym Space
excerpt: Getting a complete training offer into a tight footprint — what to combine, what to drop, and what never to compromise.
keywords: small gym layout, compact gym equipment, gym space planning

body.v: Small floors fail for a predictable reason: they are equipped like large floors, only with less space between things. The fix is to change the equipment strategy, not to shrink the gaps.
Combine movement patterns into fewer stations

Multi stations and multi gyms exist precisely for this. A single frame covering lat pull down, low row, chest press and leg extension replaces four footprints with one. On a tight floor this is the highest-value decision you can make.
Dual-function selectorised stations — leg curl and leg extension, inner and outer thigh, pearl delt and pec fly — apply the same logic at station level.
Go vertical with storage
Dumbbell racks, plate trees and barbell stands recover a surprising amount of usable floor. Loose weights on the floor are both a hazard and a space cost.
Choose adjustable over dedicated
One adjustable bench with a rack does the work of a flat, an incline and a decline bench. Adjustable equipment is almost always the right answer when floor area is the binding constraint.
Be honest about cardio

Cardio has the largest footprint per unit. On a small floor, two well-specified treadmills and a couple of compact bikes will serve members better than five cramped machines with no walking space. Upright bikes and spin bikes have a much smaller footprint than treadmills or cross trainers.
What not to compromise

v: Circulation. A clear route from entrance to every zone. If members have to squeeze past a machine in use, the layout is wrong.
Loading clearance. Plate-loaded stations and racks need room to load, unload and step away.
Emergency egress. Never plan a machine into an exit route, whatever it does to the equipment count.

body.v: A workable small-floor mix

For a compact commercial or society gym: one multi station, one or two treadmills, one or two bikes, an adjustable bench with rack, a dumbbell set on a rack, and a mat area. That covers every major movement pattern and still leaves room to move.
Work out your real usable area first

Measure the room, then subtract everything you cannot use: the door swing, the circulation route from entrance to every zone, the space in front of mirrors, and any structural column with its clearance. What is left is what you are actually equipping, and it is usually 25–30% less than the floor plan suggests.
Plan against that number. Planning against the gross area is how small floors end up with no room to walk.
Use height as well as floor

Wall-mounted storage, vertical plate trees, dumbbell racks and stacked bench storage all convert floor area into wall area. On a tight floor this is the difference between a room that feels equipped and one that feels cluttered.

Check ceiling height before specifying anything with a lat tower or a smith machine. Under about 3 m, several categories simply stop being options — and finding that out after ordering is an expensive way to learn it.
Sequence the floor for flow

In a small room, people bump into each other. Reduce it by grouping stations so a member can complete a session without crossing the room repeatedly: pushing movements together, pulling together, legs together, and the mat area out of the main walkway.
Put the noisiest equipment — air bikes, free weights — furthest from the entrance, so the room does not feel chaotic the moment someone walks in.
A worked example: a 40 m² society gym

v: One multi station covering press, pull, row and leg work — one footprint, most of the strength coverage
Two treadmills, or one treadmill and one cross trainer if the room is narrow
One upright or recumbent bike — recumbent if the residents skew older
One adjustable bench with a rack
A dumbbell set on a vertical rack
A matted area of around 6 m² for stretching and floor work
Wall mirrors on the longest wall, and a clear walkway throughout

body.v: That covers every major movement pattern, serves a realistic peak of six to eight people, and still leaves room to move. Adding two more machines to the same room would serve fewer people, not more.
What small floors should not compromise

Circulation, loading clearance and emergency egress. If a member has to squeeze past a machine in use to reach another, or step into someone's working space, or if any equipment sits in an exit route, the layout is wrong regardless of how many machines it fits.
Send us the dimensions of your room and we will propose a layout that fits. Get a layout and quote.

title: Gym Equipment Maintenance Guide
excerpt: A realistic maintenance routine — daily, weekly, monthly and annual — that prevents most of the faults that take machines off the floor.
keywords: gym equipment maintenance, treadmill maintenance, gym machine servicing

body.v: Almost every emergency service call we see could have been a five-minute task three months earlier. Maintenance is not complicated; it is just easy to skip.
Daily

v: Wipe down upholstery, grips and consoles — sweat is corrosive
Clear the area around and under cardio machines
Check for and report any unusual noise, vibration or belt slip
Return plates, dumbbells and collars to their storage

body.v: Weekly

v: Vacuum around and beneath treadmill motor covers — dust is the main enemy of a treadmill motor
Check treadmill belt tracking and tension
Inspect cables and pulleys on selectorised stations for fraying or stiffness
Check that every weight-stack pin is present and undamaged
Tighten visible fasteners on benches, racks and stands

body.v: Monthly

v: Lubricate treadmill decks per the model requirement — some models include a self-lubrication function operated from the control board
Check pedal, crank and saddle fixings on all bikes
Inspect frame welds and paintwork for damage or corrosion
Test emergency stop keys on every treadmill
Check guards and covers are secure on all strength stations

body.v: Annually

v: Full professional service on cardio equipment
Cable replacement assessment on high-use selectorised stations
Electrical safety check of the cardio bank
Review your spares float against actual failures over the year

body.v: The three faults worth preventing
Treadmill deck wear. Caused by running a dry deck. It destroys belts and eventually motors. Lubrication schedule, no exceptions.
Cable failure on selectorised stations. Cables fray gradually and visibly. Weekly inspection catches it; a snapped cable under load does not give warning.
Dust in motor compartments. Especially in dusty urban environments. Ten minutes with a vacuum every week extends motor life materially.
Keep a log

One sheet per machine with model number, install date, service dates and faults. When something does fail, the log turns a diagnostic conversation into a parts order — and it is what lets a warranty claim proceed without argument.
Who does what

A maintenance routine that depends on one motivated person collapses when that person leaves. Assign the daily and weekly tasks to a named role rather than a name — floor staff, duty manager — and put the checklist on the wall of the staff area, not in a file nobody opens.
Monthly and annual work usually needs a technician. Book those in advance as a recurring appointment rather than calling when something breaks.
Keep a log per machine

One sheet per machine: model number, serial number, installation date, service dates, faults and parts fitted. It takes minutes to maintain and does three things — it turns a diagnostic phone call into a parts order, it supports a warranty claim without argument, and it shows you which machines are genuinely costing you money.
After a year the log will usually reveal that a small number of machines account for most of your service spend. That is useful information the next time you specify.
Treadmills: the detail that matters most

Running a dry deck is what destroys treadmills. The belt and deck wear against each other, the friction load rises, the motor works harder, and eventually the motor fails — a large bill caused by a small omission.

Follow the lubrication interval for your model. Some Avon models include a self-lubrication function operated from the control board, applied once within about 30 days or as required; others need manual lubrication. Either way, put it on the schedule and record it in the log.

Dust is the second enemy. In urban Maharashtra, motor compartments fill quickly. Ten minutes with a vacuum every week extends motor life materially, and it is the single highest-value maintenance task in the building.
Selectorised stations: watch the cables

Cables fray gradually and visibly at the pulleys before they fail. A weekly visual inspection catches it; a cable that snaps under load gives no warning and is a genuine injury risk. Replace at the first sign of fraying rather than at failure, and keep a spare set for your highest-use stations.
Check guards and covers are secure at the same time. A missing guard on a moving stack is the most common avoidable hazard on a gym floor.
Monsoon and coastal maintenance

Humidity along the Maharashtra coast and through the monsoon accelerates corrosion on fixings and any chipped paintwork. Add a post-monsoon inspection to the annual routine: check fixings for rust, touch up damaged powder coating before it spreads, and pay particular attention to anything installed outdoors.
Hold a spares float

Keep a small stock of the items that stop a machine being usable but take minutes to fit: treadmill safety keys, weight-stack pins, collars, and a spare set of cables for your busiest stations. These are inexpensive, and holding them converts a week of downtime into ten minutes.
We support the equipment we install. Service and spares.

title: How to Choose Strength Training Equipment
excerpt: Selectorised, plate-loaded and free weights — what each format is good at, and how to combine them on one floor.
keywords: strength training equipment, selectorised gym equipment, plate loaded machines, multi station

body.v: Strength equipment comes in three formats, and the mistake is treating them as competitors rather than as tools for different jobs.
Selectorised (pin-loaded) stations

A weight stack, a pin and a guided path. Fast to adjust, safe to use unsupervised, and the backbone of any general-fitness floor. Look at the stack rating (100 kg and 110 kg are common in the Avon range), cable thickness, frame tube specification and the quality of guards and upholstery.
Cost more per station than plate-loaded, but they keep a busy floor moving because changing weight takes two seconds.
Plate-loaded stations

The frame guides the movement; you add Olympic plates for resistance. Lower cost per station, higher top-end loading, and preferred by experienced lifters for the loading feel. The trade-off is plate handling, plate storage and slower changeovers.
If you go plate-loaded, budget for the plates and for enough storage trees that plates are not left on the floor.
Free weights

Benches, racks, dumbbells, barbells and plates. The lowest cost per unit of training value and the highest demand from experienced members — but they need the most floor area, the most supervision and proper rubber flooring underneath.
Multi stations and multi gyms
Several exercises on one frame with one or more stacks. The right answer for small floors, home gyms and society gyms, where footprint is the binding constraint.
Covering the movement patterns
Rather than counting machines, check you can train each pattern:

v: Horizontal push — chest press
Horizontal pull — seated row
Vertical push — shoulder press
Vertical pull — lat pull down
Knee-dominant — leg press, leg extension
Hip-dominant — leg curl, glute work
Core — abdominal isolator or equivalent

body.v: If every pattern is covered, a small floor will feel complete. If three machines cover the same pattern, a large floor will still feel thin.
What to check on the specification

v: Frame tube — high-tensile steel is the commercial standard
Finish — a two-round powder coating holds up to sweat and cleaning
Cable — 6 mm is typical on commercial selectorised stations
Upholstery — PU leatherised pads are serviceable and replaceable
Guards — impact-resistant thermoplastic or steel covers over moving parts

body.v: How many stations do you actually need?

Work from your busiest hour. If twenty people are training strength at peak and a set plus rest runs three minutes, a single station serves roughly twenty people an hour — but only if nobody wants it at the same moment. In practice, duplicate the three that always queue (chest press, lat pull down, leg press) and single-up the rest.

Then check coverage rather than count. A floor with every movement pattern covered once feels complete; a floor with three machines doing horizontal pressing and nothing for hip-dominant work does not, however many machines it has.
Reading a strength specification

v: Frame tube: high-tensile steel is the commercial standard. This is the structural claim, and it is the one that matters over ten years.
Weight stack: 100 kg and 110 kg are common in the Avon commercial range. Check it suits your strongest members, not your average one.
Cable: 6 mm is typical on commercial selectorised stations. Thinner cable on a commercial floor is a false economy.
Finish: a two-round powder coating survives sweat and daily cleaning far better than a single coat.
Upholstery: PU leatherised pads are serviceable and replaceable — check that they are a replaceable panel, not a bonded assembly.
Guards: impact-resistant thermoplastic or steel covers over moving parts and stacks.

body.v: Ergonomics: the thing you can only test in person

A station with the right specification can still be wrong if the movement path does not suit your members. Check the range of seat and pad adjustment, whether a short user and a tall user can both set up correctly, and whether the starting position is reachable without an awkward entry.

Dual-function stations — leg curl and extension, inner and outer thigh, pearl delt and pec fly — halve the footprint but need more adjustment between users. On a busy floor that trade-off is worth understanding before you commit.
Free weights: what the area actually needs

A free-weight area is not just benches and dumbbells. It needs rubber flooring heavy enough to protect the slab, enough storage that nothing lives on the floor, clearance around every rack for a spotter and the bar path, and ideally a sightline from reception because it is the zone where supervision matters most.
Budget the flooring and the storage as part of the free-weight decision, not as an afterthought. They are what make the difference between an area that works and one that is a hazard.
Mixing series on one floor

Avon manufactures several commercial strength series, each covering a set of stations built to a consistent frame and finish specification. Equipping from one series gives a floor that reads as a coherent set. Mixing series is perfectly workable and common — it is a styling decision, not a compatibility one — and lets you put budget where the usage actually is.
Browse by series or by station: strength equipment, multi stations, multi gyms.

title: Complete Home Gym Equipment Guide
excerpt: Building a home gym that gets used — what to buy first, what to add later, and what most people regret.
keywords: home gym equipment, home gym setup India, best home gym equipment

body.v: The most common home gym mistake is buying a large cardio machine first, using it for six weeks, and then owning a clothes rail. A home gym gets used when it matches how you actually train.
Start with the question, not the catalogue
What do you want to be able to do in twelve months? Run further, get stronger, move better after sitting all day, or rehabilitate something? Each answer leads to a different first purchase.
If your goal is cardio

A folding treadmill is the obvious choice and a good one if you will genuinely run. Look at running area and user weight rating — domestic models around 1200–1300 mm long and rated near 110–130 kg suit most households. Folding by cylinder matters if the room has another use.
If joints are a concern, a cross trainer or a recumbent bike is a better first machine. Recumbent bikes in particular are easy to get on and off and comfortable enough that they actually get used.
If your goal is strength
A home gym station or multi gym covers the main movement patterns in one footprint with no loose plates and no spotter required. For most homes this beats assembling a free-weight setup.
If you have the space and the experience, an adjustable bench, a rack and a dumbbell set will take you further for the same money — but only if you already know how to train with them.
The sequence that works

v: First: one main machine matched to your primary goal
Second: a mat, and an adjustable bench or a set of dumbbells
Third: storage — a rack or stand, so the room stays usable
Later: accessories for variety — bands, ropes, ab wheel, kettlebells

body.v: Practical checks before you order

v: Measure the room including ceiling height and the swing of the door
Check the machine will get up your stairs or into your lift — check gross weight too
Confirm a power socket within reach for any motorised machine
For upper floors, consider matting to reduce noise and vibration for neighbours

body.v: What people regret
Buying the biggest machine that fits rather than the one they will use; skipping storage and losing the room; and choosing on programme count rather than on comfort and footprint.
Room, floor and noise

Three practical checks before you choose anything. Ceiling height decides whether a lat tower or functional trainer is even possible. Floor type decides whether you need matting — on tiles or a wooden floor you do, both to protect the surface and to stop the machine walking under load.

Noise matters more than people expect, particularly in apartments. If you train early or late, or live above someone, favour magnetic-resistance bikes and cross trainers over treadmills and air bikes, and put matting under everything.
Access: measure before you order

Check the door width, the narrowest point of the staircase including the turn, and, if relevant, the lift's internal dimensions and rated capacity. Compare against the machine's gross weight and assembled dimensions, both of which are published on each product page.
Many domestic treadmills fold by cylinder for storage, which helps a great deal in a room that has another use — but a folding machine still has to get into the room in the first place.
A realistic first-year plan

v: Month 1: the main machine for your primary goal, plus a mat
Month 3: an adjustable bench, or a dumbbell set with a rack
Month 6: storage — the point at which the room stops working is the point you ran out of places to put things
Month 12: accessories for variety: bands, a rope, an ab wheel, kettlebells

body.v: Buying in this order means each purchase is made by someone who now knows how they actually train, rather than how they imagined they would.
Home maintenance takes ten minutes a month

Wipe down after use — sweat corrodes. Check fixings on benches and racks monthly, because they loosen. Lubricate a treadmill deck to the schedule for your model; some include a self-lubrication function from the console. Vacuum around and beneath the motor compartment.
That routine is the difference between a machine that lasts a decade and one that develops a noise in year two.
Two honest cautions

First, the machine that gets used is the one you want to use. A treadmill bought because it is the obvious choice, by someone who dislikes running, is furniture. Be honest about that before you order.

Second, do not put domestic equipment into a shared gym. Society gyms and building fitness rooms look like light use but are unsupervised and used by many households — a commercial pattern. That is a different specification, and getting it wrong shows up within a year.

title: Gym Equipment for Hotels and Resorts
excerpt: Guest fitness rooms have different constraints to gyms. Footprint, finish, noise and unsupervised safety all outrank raw capability.
keywords: hotel gym equipment, resort fitness centre equipment, hospitality gym setup

body.v: A hotel fitness room is not a small gym. It is an unsupervised amenity used by guests of unknown training background, often early in the morning, usually directly above or below a guest room.
Footprint comes first

Hotel fitness rooms are almost always a converted space with awkward dimensions. Compact cardio — upright bikes, recumbent bikes, cross trainers — delivers more usable options per square metre than a row of treadmills. Multi stations cover strength in a single footprint.
Noise and vibration

This is the complaint that reaches the general manager. Choose quieter drive systems, specify proper matting under every machine, and avoid placing high-impact equipment directly above guest rooms. Fan-resistance air bikes are excellent training tools and a poor hospitality choice for this reason.
Unsupervised safety

There is no instructor on the floor at 6 am. That argues for selectorised and guided equipment over free weights, clear instruction placards on every machine, working emergency stop keys on treadmills, and conservative loading options.
Finish quality

Guests judge the room in the first three seconds. Frame finish, upholstery condition and console cleanliness matter more here than on a gym floor where members forgive wear. Powder-coated frames and replaceable PU upholstery keep the room presentable over a longer life.
A workable hotel specification

v: One or two treadmills, well specified rather than numerous
One cross trainer and one recumbent or upright bike
One multi station covering the main movement patterns
An adjustable bench and a compact dumbbell set on a rack
Mats, and mirrors on at least one wall

body.v: That fits a modest room, covers every guest need, and stays presentable.
Maintenance access
Plan service access from day one. A machine wedged into a corner is a machine that stays broken longer, and an out-of-order sign in a hotel gym is seen by every guest.
Sizing the room honestly

Most hotel fitness rooms are a converted space with awkward dimensions, a column in the wrong place and no natural ventilation. Work from what the room can genuinely hold with clearances, not from a target machine count — five machines with room to move reads as a better facility than eight crammed in.
Mirrors on one wall make a modest room feel considerably larger, and they are the cheapest improvement available.
Occupancy drives the specification

A 40-room business hotel and a 300-room resort need different rooms. Business hotels see concentrated early-morning use by a small proportion of guests; resorts see lighter, more spread-out use across a wider age range. The first needs throughput at 6–8 am; the second needs accessibility and variety.
Hours, access and liability

If the room is open 24 hours with keycard access, everything about the specification tightens: no loose plates, guided equipment only, working emergency stops on every treadmill, clear instruction placards, and a visible emergency contact. Anything a guest can misuse unsupervised, they eventually will.
Check the equipment list against your insurer's requirements before you order rather than after.
Cleaning and presentation

Housekeeping, not gym staff, will clean this room. That argues for finishes that survive general-purpose cleaning products, upholstery that wipes down without marking, and consoles without fabric or open seams. Provide sanitiser and towels at the entrance — guests notice their absence immediately.
A specification that works for most hotels

v: One or two treadmills — specified well rather than numerous
One cross trainer, for low-impact and older guests
One recumbent or upright bike, compact and quiet
One multi station covering the main movement patterns
An adjustable bench and a small dumbbell set on a rack
Mats, mirrors, a water point and a clock

body.v: That fits a modest room, covers essentially every guest requirement, needs no supervision and stays presentable — which is the actual brief.
Plan service access from day one

A machine wedged into a corner is a machine that stays broken longer, and an out-of-order sign in a hotel gym is seen by every guest who opens the door. Leave working space behind and beside each unit, and agree a service response expectation with your supplier before the room opens.

title: Gym Equipment for Corporate Fitness Centres
excerpt: Office gyms live or die on peak-hour throughput and near-zero maintenance overhead. Specify for that, not for a commercial club.
keywords: corporate gym equipment, office fitness centre, workplace gym setup

body.v: A corporate fitness centre has an unusual usage pattern: almost nothing for most of the day, then everything at once before work, at lunch and after work. Specify for the peak, not the average.
Throughput beats variety

At 6 pm, twenty people want to train in the same hour. Selectorised stations win decisively here — changing weight takes two seconds instead of loading and unloading plates. Duplicate the most-used stations rather than adding exotic ones that sit idle.
Design for the deconditioned

Corporate populations skew towards people returning to training after years at a desk. Guided, selectorised equipment with clear instruction is safer and less intimidating than a free-weight area. Recumbent bikes and cross trainers get used by people who would never step onto a treadmill.
Maintenance overhead must be near zero
There is rarely dedicated gym staff. That means:

v: Equipment with simple controls that do not need explaining
Minimal loose components — plates and collars go missing without supervision
Robust finishes that survive cleaning by general facilities staff
An annual maintenance contract rather than reactive call-outs

body.v: Space is usually borrowed

Corporate gyms are typically fitted into a converted meeting room or basement area with fixed columns and low ceilings. Multi stations and compact cardio matter more than on a purpose-built floor. Check ceiling height against any lat tower or functional trainer before specifying it.
A workable corporate specification

For a mid-size office: two or three treadmills, two cross trainers, two upright or recumbent bikes, one or two multi stations, an adjustable bench, a compact dumbbell set on a rack, and a matted stretching area. That handles a peak hour without queues and needs almost no supervision.
Model the peak, not the headcount

A thousand-person office does not need a thousand-person gym. What it needs is enough positions to absorb the 6 pm surge without a queue that sends people home. Count the realistic peak — typically a small percentage of headcount, concentrated into three windows a day — and specify for that.
Getting this wrong in either direction is costly: under-specify and the facility gets a reputation for queues; over-specify and you have paid for equipment that is idle 90% of the day.
Equipment that does not need explaining

There is usually nobody on the floor to show someone how a machine works. That argues for guided, selectorised stations with clear instruction placards, conservative loading increments, and consoles with obvious controls.

It also argues against a large free-weight area. Free weights give the most training value per rupee and need the most supervision — in an unsupervised corporate room, that trade-off usually does not work.
The space is almost always borrowed

Corporate gyms get fitted into converted meeting rooms, basement areas and odd corners with fixed columns and low ceilings. Measure ceiling height before specifying anything with a lat tower or smith machine, and expect to use multi stations rather than separate machines.
Check the access route too. Basement and upper-floor conversions are exactly where a 250 kg selectorised station becomes a logistics problem.
Facilities, not fitness, will run it

v: Specify finishes that survive general-purpose cleaning products
Minimise loose components — collars and pins disappear without supervision
Put an annual maintenance contract in place rather than relying on call-outs
Leave a laminated maintenance checklist in the room
Provide a clear point of contact for reporting a fault

body.v: Accessibility widens usage more than variety does

Corporate populations skew towards people returning to training after years at a desk, and often span a wide age range. A recumbent bike and a cross trainer will be used by people who would never step onto a treadmill, and guided stations will be used by people who would never approach a squat rack.
If the goal is participation rather than performance, accessibility is the specification decision that moves the number.

title: Outdoor Gym Equipment Guide
excerpt: Open-air fitness for parks, societies and campuses — what to install, how to fix it down, and what keeps it working.
keywords: outdoor gym equipment, open gym park equipment, housing society gym, community fitness

body.v: Outdoor gym equipment succeeds when it is genuinely usable by the people who walk past it every day — which usually means older residents, beginners and children, not trained lifters.
Where it works

v: Housing societies. A small cluster near a walking path gets used far more than a large installation in a far corner.
Public parks. Municipal fitness zones, usually alongside a jogging track.
Campuses. Schools, colleges and institutional grounds.
Resorts and community spaces. An amenity that needs no supervision and no power.

body.v: What to install

Outdoor equipment uses body weight and mechanical resistance rather than weight stacks. Typical units cover walking and stepping motion, upper-body pulling and pushing, seated leg work, twisting and core movement, and shoulder mobility. A balanced cluster of six to ten units serves a society or park well.
Choose a spread across lower body, upper body and mobility rather than several units doing the same thing.
Foundations are not optional

This is where outdoor installations most often go wrong. Every unit needs a proper concrete foundation sized for it and cured before use. Equipment bolted to a thin slab or set in inadequate footings becomes unsafe quickly. Foundation components are part of the order, not an afterthought — we supply them alongside the units.
Siting

v: Near a walking route, where people already go
Partial shade if possible — metal in direct Maharashtra summer sun gets hot
On level ground with drainage, not in a spot that floods in monsoon
With clear space around each unit for safe movement
Visible from occupied areas, which discourages misuse

body.v: Monsoon and maintenance

Maharashtra weather is the real test. Check fixings and paintwork after every monsoon, treat any corrosion before it spreads, and keep moving joints clean. Instruction signage at each unit is worth installing — most misuse comes from not knowing how a unit is meant to work.
Choosing a balanced cluster

The common mistake is installing six units that all work the same thing. Spread the selection across lower body (walkers, steppers, leg press), upper body (pull-down and push stations, arm wheels), and mobility and core (twisters, waist units, shoulder wheels).
Six to ten well-chosen units serve a society or a neighbourhood park properly. Twenty units in a far corner of the grounds will be used less than six beside the walking path.
Foundations in detail

Each unit needs its own concrete foundation, sized for that unit and fully cured before anyone uses it. Equipment bolted to a thin slab, or set into footings that have not cured, becomes unsafe quickly — and outdoor equipment is used unsupervised, so "unsafe quickly" is a real problem rather than a theoretical one.

Foundation components are supplied with the equipment. What the site must provide is level, drained ground and access for the installation team. Agree who is doing the excavation and concreting before the delivery date.
Safety surfacing and spacing

Leave genuine clear space around each unit — enough that someone using one is not in the working path of the next. Where budget allows, rubber or soft surfacing under and around the units reduces injury risk and is worth prioritising where children will use the area.
Install instruction signage at each unit. Most outdoor equipment misuse is not carelessness; it is people not knowing how a unit is meant to work.
Surviving the Maharashtra monsoon

This is the real durability test. Build a post-monsoon inspection into the annual routine: check every fixing for corrosion, check moving joints for stiffness and grit, and treat any chipped paintwork before rust spreads under the coating.
Standing water is the other issue. Equipment installed in a spot that floods will corrode from the base up regardless of finish quality, so drainage is a siting decision, not a maintenance one.
Getting it used

v: Site it where people already walk, not where there is spare space
Keep it visible from occupied buildings — visibility discourages misuse
Provide partial shade if the site allows; metal in full summer sun gets hot
Add a water point and a bench nearby if you can
Tell residents it exists — an opening notice genuinely increases usage

body.v: An outdoor gym is one of the cheapest fitness amenities available per person served. It fails almost exclusively for siting and maintenance reasons, not equipment ones.
See the range: outdoor gym equipment.

title: How to Plan a Commercial Gym Floor
excerpt: Zoning, circulation, sightlines and clearances — how equipment gets arranged so a floor works at its busiest.
keywords: commercial gym floor plan, gym layout planning, gym zoning

body.v: A gym floor plan is a circulation problem with equipment in it. Judge every layout decision by what happens at your busiest hour, not by how it looks empty.
Zone the floor

v: Entrance and reception. Clear sightline into the gym.
Cardio. Near ventilation and natural light; the most visible zone from the door.
Selectorised strength. Central, where circulation is easiest and supervision is simplest.
Free weights and racks. Against a structural wall, on rubber flooring, away from main walkways.
Functional and stretching. A defined open area that is not a through-route.

body.v: Circulation

Plan a main walkway wide enough for two people to pass comfortably, running from the entrance through the floor. No machine should require a member to step into someone else's working space to reach it. If the only way to the leg press is between two benches in use, the layout needs changing.
Clearances
Footprint is not the space a machine needs. Add:

v: Behind treadmills: run-off space, both for safety and for service access
Around plate-loaded stations: room to load, unload and step clear
Around racks: room for a spotter and for the bar path
Behind selectorised stations: access to the stack and guards for maintenance

body.v: As a planning rule of thumb, total floor area tends to run 40–50% above the sum of equipment footprints once circulation and clearances are included.
Sightlines

Staff should be able to see most of the floor from reception. Position tall equipment against walls rather than through the middle, so the floor does not become a set of blind corridors. This matters for safety and for the feeling of space.
Grouping by pattern

Group stations so a member can complete a session without crossing the floor repeatedly — pushing movements together, pulling together, leg stations together. It reduces congestion and makes the floor feel organised.
Services

Mark power sockets for the cardio bank on the drawing, along with mirror positions, storage racks, water points and the fire exit route. Equipment must never obstruct egress, whatever it does to the machine count.
Start with the constraints, not the equipment

Before placing a single machine, mark on the drawing everything you cannot move: structural columns, the fire exit route, ventilation positions, windows, the entrance, and the route to changing rooms. What remains is the floor you are actually planning.
Plan the circulation next, then place equipment into what is left. Planning equipment first and circulation second is how floors end up with no clear walkway.
Clearance figures worth designing to

v: Main walkway: wide enough for two people to pass without turning sideways
Behind treadmills: run-off space for safety, plus room to service the motor compartment
Around racks: room for a spotter and the full bar path in every direction
Plate-loaded stations: room to load, unload and step clear without entering the next station
Selectorised stations: access behind for the stack and guards
Mat and functional area: a defined zone that is not a through-route

body.v: Floor loading and services

A selectorised station with a full stack can exceed 250 kg gross in a single footprint, and a rack loaded with plates concentrates more. On upper floors, particularly in older buildings, have the loading checked against the equipment schedule before you commit.
Mark power sockets for the cardio bank, water points, mirror positions and storage on the same drawing. Every one of those is cheap to place now and expensive to add after flooring.
Flooring by zone

Flooring is part of the layout, not a finish applied afterwards. Free-weight areas need heavy rubber matting to protect the slab and the equipment. Cardio needs a stable, level surface. Functional and stretching areas need something comfortable to work on directly.
Mark the zones on the drawing so your flooring contractor is working from the same plan as your equipment supplier.
Design for supervision

Staff should be able to see most of the floor from reception. Position tall equipment against walls rather than through the middle, so the room does not become a set of blind corridors. Keep the free-weight area — where supervision matters most — within a clear sightline.
Test the plan before you order

Walk the drawing as a member would. Enter, get to the changing room, get to cardio, move to three strength stations in sequence, reach the water point, reach the exit. If any of those routes crosses someone else's working space, adjust the layout — it is free to do now, and it is the single thing members will notice every day for years.

title: Gym Equipment Checklist for New Gym Owners
excerpt: A working checklist covering equipment, accessories, infrastructure and the operational items that get forgotten.
keywords: gym equipment checklist, new gym owner, gym opening checklist

body.v: Use this as a working list when you scope your first floor. The categories most often missed are at the bottom — and they are the ones that cause opening-week problems.
Cardio

v: Treadmills
Cross trainers / ellipticals
Spin bikes
Upright bikes
Recumbent bikes (accessibility and rehabilitation)
Air bike or conditioning piece

body.v: Selectorised strength

v: Chest press
Shoulder press
Lat pull down
Seated row
Leg press
Leg curl and leg extension
Abdominal isolator
Inner / outer thigh
Biceps and triceps stations

body.v: Free weights

v: Adjustable benches
Flat and incline benches
Power rack or squat rack
Smith machine or functional trainer
Dumbbell set with rack
Olympic bars and plates
Plate storage trees
Collars

body.v: Functional

v: Battle ropes
Medicine balls
Kettlebells
Mats
Resistance bands
Ab wheel and core accessories

body.v: Infrastructure — usually underestimated

v: Rubber flooring, especially under free weights
Mirrors
Ventilation and fans
Electrical supply sized for the cardio bank, with sockets positioned on the layout
Water point and waste bins
Storage for towels and cleaning supplies

body.v: Operational — the genuinely forgotten list

v: Instruction placards for each machine
First aid kit and emergency procedure
Cleaning stations and sanitiser for members
Maintenance log sheets per machine
A small spares float — treadmill safety keys, collars, weight-stack pins
Signage for the free-weight area and emergency exits

body.v: Before you sign the order

v: Confirm every machine fits through your access route — check gross weight, not just dimensions
Confirm the layout drawing matches the equipment list
Confirm installation and commissioning are included in the quotation
Confirm warranty terms and who to call for service
Confirm delivery timing against your flooring and electrical schedule

body.v: How to use this list

Do not treat it as a shopping list to buy in full. Work through it in three passes: mark what your concept genuinely requires, mark what can wait to phase two, and mark what does not apply. What survives the first pass is your opening order.
Pre-order checks, in order

v: Access. Lift internal dimensions and rated capacity, staircase width including the turn, doorway width — checked against each machine's assembled dimensions and gross weight.
Ceiling height. Decides whether functional trainers, smith machines and lat towers are possible at all.
Floor loading. Particularly on upper floors in older buildings.
Electrical supply. Sized against the actual cardio list, with socket positions on the layout drawing.
Layout signed off. Zoning, circulation and clearances agreed in writing before anything ships.

body.v: Questions to ask before signing

v: Is the quotation by model number, with published specifications attached?
Are delivery, installation and commissioning included, or extra?
What is the warranty on each product line, in writing?
Where do spares come from and what is a realistic wait for a common part?
Who physically attends site for a service call?
What is the lead time, and what happens if site readiness slips?

body.v: A supplier who answers all six clearly is one you can plan around. A quotation that is a list of category names and one total is not something you can evaluate at all.
Opening-week items people forget

v: Instruction placards fitted to every machine
First aid kit, and a written emergency procedure
Cleaning stations and sanitiser for members
Maintenance log sheets, one per machine, with model and serial numbers
A spares float: treadmill safety keys, weight-stack pins, collars
Signage for the free-weight area and the emergency exits
Somewhere to put the packaging — a full commercial order generates a lot

body.v: Your first 90 days

Start the maintenance routine on day one rather than when something breaks. Record every fault, however minor. Watch where queues actually form — it will not be where you predicted — and let that, not a plan drawn before you opened, decide what you add in phase two.

After three months you will know which machines your members actually use, which ones cost you service time, and where the floor is tight. That is far better information to buy on than anything available before opening.
